assumptions.A1: Every Early Decision admit enrolls. ED is binding; in practice a few are released, mostly for financial aid.
assumptions.A2: Seats left for everyone outside ED = enrolled first-years minus ED admits.
assumptions.A3: A group's advantage (women or men, in-state, out-of-state, international) is the same in every round. Colleges report these splits for all applicants together, not by round.
assumptions.A4: Group factors combine by multiplying, as if sex and residency were independent.
assumptions.A5: Where a college does not report its Early Action round separately, EA and regular applicants are taken to be admitted at the same rate. At most colleges EA admits at a higher rate, so this understates EA odds.
assumptions.A6: Test score factor (rule of thumb): odds double for a score one middle-50% width above the middle of the range and halve one width below, capped between ×0.3 and ×2.5. Published research (Chetty, Deming and Friedman, 2023) finds admit rates at selective colleges rise steadily with scores; the exact slope here is our assumption.
assumptions.A7: When a college did not report a number this year, we use the same college's nearest year; failing that, the median of similar colleges (same admit-rate band).
assumptions.A8: Recruited athletes, legacies and other favoured applicants sit inside these pools and are admitted at much higher rates, so an unhooked applicant's odds are lower than the pool's.
assumptions.A10: Applying without a test score is treated like a score at the 25th percentile of students who sent one (×0.71 on the A6 scale), and ×0.3 where nearly everyone enrolled sent a score. Colleges do not publish admit rates for applicants without scores in the Common Data Set; where the numbers can be worked out (for example Barnard), applicants without scores did somewhat less well than those with them.
assumptions.A11: Factors multiply the odds (chance of yes ÷ chance of no), not the percentage, so a college that admits most applicants cannot be pushed past 100%. At low admit rates this is the same as multiplying the percentage. Colleges where almost no enrolled students sent a score are treated as test-blind: no score adjustment either way.
assumptions.A12: Early Decision pools include recruited athletes, legacies and other hooked applicants, who are admitted at far higher rates and mostly apply early. For your Early Decision odds we take out an estimated hooked share of ED admits (30% at colleges admitting under 15%, 20% at 15-35%, 10% above) admitted at about 75%, and use what is left: the unhooked ED rate, never below the rate for everyone else. Basis: Arcidiacono, Kinsler & Ransom, Legacy and Athlete Preferences at Harvard (NBER w26316): recruited athletes, legacies, dean's list and faculty children are about 30% of Harvard admits and over 43% of white admits; Chetty, Deming & Friedman (NBER w31492): legacies and recruited athletes are admitted at several times the rate of comparable applicants at Ivy-Plus colleges. The college's reported ED rate is shown unchanged everywhere else.
assumptions.A9: Trends are straight lines fitted to up to seven years (2018-19 on). A trend is called clear when the line explains at least 60% of the year-to-year change; the projection extends that line one year.
